items.title: How to spot real Black Friday savings this holiday season amid the affordability squeeze
items.summary:
Black Friday deals are everywhere, but a sale price does not always mean real savings.

With budgets under pressure, amid a persisting affordability crisis and rising fuel prices with the raging Iran conflict, shoppers are looking for ways to stretch their money during the holiday shopping season this year.

The forecasts point to a season of cautious spending. Visa Business and Economics Insights expects holiday sales to increase 4.5% from last year — but after accounting for higher prices, the actual increase in what shoppers buy is projected to be just 1.1%.

That makes it all the more important for shoppers to know what they’re paying for and whether a sale is truly a deal.

"It's still a good time to shop. It's just that you just have to be a little bit more careful," Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, told Fox News Digital when discussing holiday and Black Friday shopping.

7 HOLIDAY SHOPPING SCAMS TO WATCH FOR THIS SEASON

Gauri revealed that shopping during Black Friday does not always produce the best deal — especially when it comes to essential technology like cell phones.

He advised shoppers to set a budget and research prices before making a purchase, especially for big-ticket items.

"Have a number in mind and do your research before you go about spending the money," he said, recommending price-tracking sites and extra promotions.

items.title: The most surprising thing about Burnham’s slow politics is this: it could be working | Andy Beckett
items.summary:
‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs?

Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning.

Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

items.t: The most surprising thing about Burnham’s slow politics is this: it could be working | Andy Beckett

items.title: Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Brookings Institution president, dies at 80
items.summary:
Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped U.S. foreign policy before he went on to lead the Brookings Institution, died Thursday at the age of 80.

Talbott’s son, Devin Talbott, said his father died peacefully after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, The Associated Press reported.

An Ohio native, Talbott began his journalism career as an intern at Time magazine while studying at Yale and Oxford, where he was roommates with future President Bill Clinton. Clinton later joked that his job in their shared apartment was to make Talbott breakfast every morning.

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

While at Time, Talbott was tapped to translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former Soviet leader ousted in 1964, which earned him a full-time role at the magazine.

Over a 21-year career there, he focused on U.S.-Soviet relations, led the Washington bureau, and wrote as a foreign affairs columnist.

In 1994, Talbott joined the Clinton administration as deputy secretary of state, helping guide U.S.…

items.title: FLASHBACK: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving surprises for US troops — see the moments
items.summary:
Under a cloak of secrecy, two American presidents made surprise Thanksgiving visits to war zones, bringing a taste of home to U.S. troops serving thousands of miles from their families.

Sixteen years apart, President George W. Bush celebrated with American troops in Iraq in 2003, while President Donald Trump served Thanksgiving dinner to service members in Afghanistan in 2019. Both visits were carried out under tight secrecy, catching troops by surprise as they spent the holiday far from home.

Trump secretly traveled to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, when he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war.

INSIDE TRUMP’S INTIMATE MEETING WITH NATION’S BRAVEST SOLDIERS DURING WHIRLWIND TEXAS TRIP

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time, later adding, "And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.
items.t: FLASHBACK: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving surprises for US troops — see the moments

items.title: Politics, money and Thanksgiving dinner: Just two words can help avoid argument
items.summary:
As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense.

Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil.

"‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation."

Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather, it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions."

If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that."

items.title: Trump country cracked: 5 races that saw double-digit Trump territory fall to Democrats in 2026

Democrats also won Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina, captured the Texas governor’s office and flipped a Republican-held House seat deep in Trump country in Indiana that had not elected a Democrat since 1990.

The results stand out for more than the presidential margins as well — Democrats broke Senate streaks that had lasted decades and defeated Republican incumbents in races many expected the GOP to hold, including one where the Democratic challenger spent next to nothing on television advertisements.

Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

items.title: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one

These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape.

To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett, was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: The census provides a critical snapshot of the US. Proposed changes could affect who is counted in 2030
items.summary:
Trump administration’s bid to cut question on race and add one on citizenship could reshape how the US population is understood

Just a few years away from the 2030 census, the US Census Bureau is considering changes that could fundamentally reshape how people are counted – and therefore impact democracy, education, infrastructure and health. The proposed rule changes would add two new parts to the regulations that govern the census: One change would remove a question about race and ethnicity, while another would add a citizenship question. Also among the proposed changes is a line that would formally bar questions about sexual orientation from being included.

The US census is critical in understanding the American population. It helps researchers understand health and social outcomes and gives legislators the data they use for legislative redistricting and congressional apportionment. But this sweeping census rule change, quietly proposed by the Trump administration before the midterm elections, could reshape US society as we know it, warn some civil rights advocates.

In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree.

Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most.

items.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew

Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television?

Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis.

items.title: Iowans anxious over lead detonation: ‘We had only five days of warning’
items.summary:
Detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide scheduled for Wednesday after several delays amid public outcry

Residents of Iowa, Illinois and Missouri who are preparing for Thanksgiving are also bracing themselves for the detonation of hazardous bomb-making materials, after the US army announced it would go through with plans for a controlled explosion on Wednesday.

The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide is now scheduled for 10am EST after being delayed several times over the past week amid public outcry and political wrangling.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan
items.summary:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan

items.title: The next fight for democracy is in the states | Stacey Abrams
items.summary:
Defend those being targeted, even when the threat has not reached your door

Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with bold ideas for America’s political future. Today’s edition was written by Stacey Abrams, a voting rights activist, author, and former Georgia house minority leader.

On 3 November, from Arizona to Georgia to Pennsylvania to Wisconsin, where a 16-year Republican majority fell, voters flipped at least 12 legislative chambers, the strongest statehouse showing for pro-democracy candidates since 2008. This did not happen by chance.

Our democracy will be measured by what we protect, what we build and whom we refuse to leave behind.

items.t: The next fight for democracy is in the states | Stacey Abrams
